text:
Answers below — all three verified against the source.

## 1. `deleteComment` — no, it does not verify authorship

There's no ownership check anywhere in the chain, and no data to check against even if you added one.

**Controller** (`src/article/article.controller.ts:84-88`):
```ts
@Delete(':slug/comments/:id')
async deleteComment(@Param() params) {
  const {slug, id} = params;
  return await this.articleService.deleteComment(slug, id);
}
```
No `@User('id')` param — the caller's identity never leaves the request. Compare `favorite`/`unFavorite`/`create` (lines 52, 94, 102), which all take `@User('id') userId`.

**Service** (`src/article/article.service.ts:114-129`): loads the article by slug, loads the comment by id, and deletes it. The only guard is `deleteIndex >= 0`, which checks that the comment belongs to *that article* — not that it belongs to *you*.

**Entity** (`src/article/comment.entity.ts:5-15`): `Comment` has `id`, `body`, and a `ManyToOne` to `ArticleEntity`. There is no author/user column. `addComment` (`article.service.ts:101-112`) only sets `comment.body`, so authorship is never recorded in the first place.

The route *is* behind `AuthMiddleware` (`src/article/article.module.ts:29`), so you must be logged in — but any logged-in user can delete any comment on any article. Authenticated, not authorized.

Same pattern applies to `PUT /articles/:slug` and `DELETE /articles/:slug` (`article.controller.ts:60, 69`) — also no ownership check, though there at least `ArticleEntity` has an `author` relation to check against.

Two smaller things in the same method: if `:id` doesn't exist, `commentRepository.findOne(id)` returns `undefined` and `comment.id` on line 118 throws a `TypeError` (500, not 404); and the `else` branch returns `{article}` with a 201, so deleting a nonexistent-on-this-article comment silently looks like success.

## 2. Profile routes with `AuthMiddleware`

`src/profile/profile.module.ts:19-23` registers exactly one matcher:

```ts
.forRoutes({path: 'profiles/:username/follow', method: RequestMethod.ALL});
```

| Route | Handler | Auth middleware |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /profiles/:username/follow` | `follow` (`profile.controller.ts:23`) | ✅ (via `RequestMethod.ALL`) |
| `DELETE /profiles/:username/follow` | `unFollow` (`profile.controller.ts:28`) | ✅ (via `RequestMethod.ALL`) |
| `GET /profiles/:username` | `getProfile` (`profile.controller.ts:18`) | ❌ not covered |

`getProfile` being uncovered is deliberate, not a gap — it's the RealWorld "optional auth" case. `@User('id')` falls through to the second branch of `src/user/user.decorator.ts:12-17`, which decodes the JWT off the header itself when `req.user` isn't set. So with a token you get `profile.following`; without one, `id` is `undefined` and `profile.following` is omitted by the `if (id)` guard at `profile.service.ts:43`.

One inconsistency worth noting: `follow` takes `@User('email')` while `unFollow` takes `@User('id')` — both work, but the service methods have divergent signatures (`follow(followerEmail, ...)` vs `unFollow(followerId, ...)`) for no real reason.

## 3. The `RO` suffix

`RO` = **Response Object**. It's documented in `.claude/knowledge/workspace.md:61-74`.

It marks the RealWorld response *envelope* — the single-key wrapper object every handler returns, rather than a bare entity:

| Interface | Shape |
|---|---|
| `ArticleRO` | `{ article: {...} }` |
| `ArticlesRO` | `{ articles: [...], articlesCount: n }` |
| `CommentsRO` | `{ comments: [...] }` |
| `UserRO` | `{ user: {..., token} }` |
| `ProfileRO` | `{ profile: {..., following} }` |

They live in `*.interface.ts` per module. Clients read `response.article.slug`, `response.user.token`, so returning a bare entity breaks every RealWorld frontend — `LESSONS.md:49-57` records this as a past bug (#57) and states the rule: a handler whose return type isn't a `*RO` interface is a bug even if it works in Postman.

Request bodies mirror it — handlers read `@Body('article')`, `@Body('user')`, `@Body('comment')`.

(Note: `ArticleRO` actually types its field as `ArticleEntity`, not the `ArticleData` interface defined just above it in `article.interface.ts:7-18` — so `ArticleData` and the local `Comment` interface are dead code, and the entity leaks its full column set into the response type.)
